title: PhysBrain 1.0 Technical Report
summary: Vision-language-action models have advanced rapidly, but robot trajectories alone provide limited coverage for learning broad physical understanding. PhysBrain 1.0 studies a complementary route: converting large-scale human egocentric video into structured physical commonsense supervision before robot adaptation. Our data engine extracts scene elements, spatial dynamics, action execution, and depth-aware relations, then turns them into question-answer supervision for training PhysBrain VLMs. The resulting physical priors are further transferred to VLA policies through a capability-preserving and language-sensitive adaptation design. Across multimodal QA benchmarks and embodied control benchmarks, including ERQA, PhysBench, SimplerEnv-WidowX, LIBERO, and RoboCasa, PhysBrain 1.0 achieves SOTA results and shows especially strong out-of-domain performance on SimplerEnv. These results suggest that scaling physical commonsense from human interaction video can provide an effective bridge from multimodal understanding to robot action.

AI.tldr: PhysBrain 1.0 converts large-scale human egocentric video into structured physical commonsense supervision via a data engine, trains VLMs on this data, and transfers learned physical priors to VLA policies, achieving SOTA on multimodal QA and embodied benchmarks with strong out-of-domain generalization.
AI.motivation: Robot trajectories alone provide limited coverage for learning broad physical understanding; the authors explore converting human egocentric video into structured physical commonsense supervision as a complementary, scalable alternative.
AI.method: A data engine extracts scene elements, spatial dynamics, action execution, and depth-aware relations from egocentric video, converts them into QA supervision for training PhysBrain VLMs, then transfers these physical priors to VLA policies via a capability-preserving, language-sensitive adaptation design.
AI.result: Achieves SOTA results on ERQA, PhysBench, SimplerEnv-WidowX, LIBERO, and RoboCasa, with particularly strong out-of-domain performance on SimplerEnv.
AI.conclusion: Scaling physical commonsense from human interaction video can provide an effective bridge from multimodal understanding to robot action.

title: Where to Perch in a Tree: Vision-Guidance for Tree-Grasping Drones
comment: Work in progress version accepted to the Recent Advances in Robotic Perception for Forestry
summary: This study demonstrates a method to locate an ideal perch location on a tree for vision-guided autonomous tree-perching drones. Various image processing algorithms, including those used for machine learning, image segmentation and binary image morphology, are implemented to assess the shape and structure of a tree. Rather than identifying the closest available branch, this study builds on vision methods by evaluating the potential of each branch, determining its suitability for perching based on factors such as branch width, slope (angle to the horizontal) and curvature. For a given tree-perching drone and a dataset of more than 10,000 urban tree images taken from February to October in a subtropical and temperate monsoon climate, the proposed method successfully produces a result for 76% of feasible targets. A feasible target defined as a tree where the branch diameters are sufficiently thick and where the available perching space is at least equal to the width of a tendon-driven grasping claw. These successful preliminary results create a foundation from which a number of identified improvements and additional features can be developed to create a generalised method; this will involve the incorporation of supplementary data from depth perception and attitude sensors to enhance the branch assessment.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a vision-guided method for autonomous tree-perching drones that evaluates branch suitability based on width, slope, and curvature, achieving 76% success on over 10,000 urban tree images.
AI.motivation: To enable drones to autonomously locate ideal perching positions on trees by assessing branch suitability beyond simply finding the closest branch.
AI.method: Implements image processing algorithms (machine learning, segmentation, binary morphology) to evaluate branch width, slope, and curvature for perching suitability.
AI.result: Achieves 76% success rate on feasible targets from a dataset of over 10,000 urban tree images collected from February to October in subtropical and temperate monsoon climates.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a foundation for developing a generalized method with additional features like depth perception and attitude sensors for improved branch assessment.

title: DeepSlide: From Artifacts to Presentation Delivery
summary: Presentations are a primary medium for scholarly communication, yet most AI slide generators optimize the artifact (a visually plausible deck) while under-optimizing the delivery process (pacing, narrative, and presentation preparation). We present DeepSlide, a human-in-the-loop multi-agent system that supports preparing the full presentation process, from requirement elicitation and time-budgeted narrative planning, to evidence-grounded slide--script generation, attention augmentation, and rehearsal support. DeepSlide integrates (i) a controllable logical-chain planner with per-node time budgets, (ii) a lightweight content-tree retriever for grounding, (iii) Markov-style sequential rendering with style inheritance, and (iv) sandboxed execution with minimal repair to ensure renderability. We further introduce a dual-scoreboard benchmark that cleanly separates static artifact quality from dynamic delivery excellence. Across 20 domains and diverse audience profiles, DeepSlide matches strong baselines on artifact quality while consistently achieving larger gains on delivery metrics, improving narrative flow, pacing precision, and slide--script synergy with clearer attention guidance.

AI.tldr: DeepSlide is a human-in-the-loop multi-agent system that generates presentations optimized for delivery quality (pacing, narrative, rehearsal) rather than just visual artifacts, outperforming baselines on narrative flow and pacing metrics across 20 domains.
AI.motivation: Existing AI slide generators focus on producing visually plausible slides but neglect the delivery process (pacing, narrative, presentation preparation), which is critical for effective scholarly communication.
AI.method: DeepSlide integrates (i) a controllable logical-chain planner with per-node time budgets, (ii) a lightweight content-tree retriever for grounding, (iii) Markov-style sequential rendering with style inheritance, and (iv) sandboxed execution with minimal repair for renderability. It uses a human-in-the-loop multi-agent architecture.
AI.result: Across 20 domains and diverse audience profiles, DeepSlide matches strong baselines on static artifact quality while achieving larger gains on delivery metrics—improving narrative flow, pacing precision, slide-script synergy, and attention guidance.
AI.conclusion: Optimizing for delivery excellence alongside artifact quality is feasible and yields better presentation preparation outcomes; the dual-scoreboard benchmark cleanly separates these two evaluation dimensions.

title: Does Theory of Mind Improvement Really Benefit Human-AI Interactions? Empirical Findings from Interactive Evaluations
summary: Improving the Theory of Mind (ToM) capability of Large Language Models (LLMs) is crucial for effective social interactions between these AI models and humans. However, the existing benchmarks often measure ToM capability improvement through story-reading, multiple-choice questions from a third-person perspective, while ignoring the first-person, dynamic, and open-ended nature of human-AI (HAI) interactions. To directly examine how ToM improvement techniques benefit HAI interactions, we first proposed the new paradigm of interactive ToM evaluation with both perspective and metric shifts. Next, following the paradigm, we conducted a systematic study of four representative ToM enhancement techniques using both four real-world datasets and a user study, covering both goal-oriented tasks (e.g., coding, math) and experience-oriented tasks (e.g., counseling). Our findings reveal that improvements on static benchmarks do not always translate to better performance in dynamic HAI interactions. This paper offers critical insights into ToM evaluation, showing the necessity of interaction-based assessments in developing next-generation, socially aware LLMs for HAI symbiosis.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a new interactive, first-person, dynamic paradigm for evaluating ToM in LLMs during human-AI interactions, and finds that improvements on static benchmarks do not necessarily translate to better performance in real HAI settings.
AI.motivation: Existing ToM benchmarks rely on static, third-person, multiple-choice story-reading tasks that fail to capture the first-person, dynamic, and open-ended nature of real human-AI interactions.
AI.method: Proposed a new interactive ToM evaluation paradigm with perspective and metric shifts; systematically studied four representative ToM enhancement techniques using four real-world datasets and a user study, covering both goal-oriented (coding, math) and experience-oriented (counseling) tasks.
AI.result: Improvements on static benchmarks do not always translate to better performance in dynamic HAI interactions.
AI.conclusion: Interaction-based assessments are necessary for developing socially aware LLMs for human-AI symbiosis.

title: SkillSmith: Compiling Agent Skills into Boundary-Guided Runtime Interfaces
summary: Recently, skills have been widely adopted in large language model (LLM)-based agent systems across various domains. In existing frameworks, skills are typically injected into the agent reasoning loop as contextual guidance once matched to a runtime task, enabling specialized task-solving capabilities. We find that this execution paradigm introduces two major sources of redundancy: irrelevant context injection and repeated skill-specific reasoning and planning. To this end, we propose SkillSmith, a boundary-first compiler-runtime framework that compiles skill packages offline into minimal executable interfaces. By extracting fine-grained operational boundaries from skills, SkillSmith enables agents to dynamically access and execute only the relevant components at runtime, thereby minimizing unnecessary context injection and redundant reasoning overhead. In the evaluation on SkillsBench benchmark, SkillSmith reduces solve-stage token usage by 57.44%, thinking iterations by 42.99%, solve time by 50.57% (2.02x faster), and token-proportional monetary cost by 57.44% compared with using raw-skills. Moreover, compiled artifacts produced by a stronger model can be reused by a smaller or more efficient runtime model, improving task accuracy in cases where raw skill interpretation fails. The source code and data are available at https://github.com/AetherHeart-AI/Aeloon.

AI.tldr: SkillSmith is a boundary-first compiler-runtime framework that reduces redundancy in LLM-based agent systems by compiling skill packages into minimal executable interfaces, achieving 57.44% less token usage, 42.99% fewer thinking iterations, 50.57% faster solve time, and enabling cross-model skill transfer.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agent systems inject full skill packages into the reasoning loop when a skill is matched, causing two major redundancies: irrelevant context injection and repeated skill-specific reasoning/planning.
AI.method: SkillSmith extracts fine-grained operational boundaries from skills offline, compiles them into minimal executable interfaces, and allows agents to dynamically access and execute only relevant components at runtime.
AI.result: On SkillsBench, SkillSmith reduces token usage by 57.44%, thinking iterations by 42.99%, solve time by 50.57% (2.02x faster), and cost by 57.44% vs. raw skills. Compiled artifacts from stronger models can be reused by smaller models, improving accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The boundary-first compilation approach effectively eliminates redundancy in skill-based agent systems and enables cross-model skill transfer, making agent systems more efficient and cost-effective.

title: LAPS: Improving Incremental LiDAR Mapping using Active Pooling and Sampling for Neural Distance Fields
summary: Neural distance fields offer a compact and continuous representation of 3D geometry, making them attractive for incremental LiDAR mapping. However, their online optimization is vulnerable to catastrophic forgetting, where new observations can degrade previously reconstructed geometry. Replay-based training is commonly used to address this issue, but existing methods typically rely on passive replay buffers and uniform sampling, which can waste memory on redundant observations and under-train poorly constrained regions. We propose LAPS, a replay management framework for incremental neural mapping that improves both replay retention and replay allocation during online updates. LAPS combines reliability-based active pooling to retain reliable historical samples under limited memory with uncertainty-guided active sampling to focus optimization on under-constrained regions. Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks show that LAPS consistently improves reconstruction completeness while maintaining competitive geometric accuracy. On Oxford Spires, it improves recall by 4.66 pp and F1-score by 3.79 pp over PIN-SLAM on the Blenheim Palace 05 sequence. We release our open source implementation at: https://github.com/dongjae0107/LAPS.

AI.tldr: LAPS is a replay management framework for incremental neural mapping that uses reliability-based active pooling and uncertainty-guided active sampling to combat catastrophic forgetting in neural distance fields for LiDAR SLAM, improving reconstruction completeness and geometric accuracy.
AI.motivation: Online optimization of neural distance fields for incremental LiDAR mapping suffers from catastrophic forgetting, where new observations degrade previously reconstructed geometry. Existing replay-based methods use passive buffers and uniform sampling, wasting memory on redundant data and under-training poorly constrained regions.
AI.method: LAPS combines (1) reliability-based active pooling to retain reliable historical samples under limited memory, and (2) uncertainty-guided active sampling to focus optimization on under-constrained regions during online updates.
AI.result: On Oxford Spires, LAPS improves recall by 4.66 pp and F1-score by 3.79 pp over PIN-SLAM on the Blenheim Palace 05 sequence. It consistently improves reconstruction completeness while maintaining competitive geometric accuracy on synthetic and real-world benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: LAPS is an effective replay management strategy for incremental neural mapping that addresses catastrophic forgetting through intelligent sample retention and allocation.

title: Fair outputs, Biased Internals: Causal Potency and Asymmetry of Latent Bias in LLMs for High-Stakes Decisions
summary: Instruction-tuned language models exhibit behavioural fairness in high-stakes decisions while retaining biased associations in their internal representations. However, whether these suppressed representations can affect model outputs - and whether such causal potency is symmetric across demographic groups - remains unknown. We investigate the use of open-weight models for mortgage underwriting using matched applications that differ only in racially-associated names and reveal a critical disconnect: models show no output-level bias, yet retain and amplify demographic representations across model layers. Through activation steering and novel cross-layer interventions, we demonstrate that this suppressed information is decision-relevant: when reinjected at critical layers, it produces near-complete decision reversals. Critically, this latent bias is asymmetric - steering interventions affect decisions in one demographic direction, while producing minimal effects in reverse - and susceptible to adversarial prompt engineering and parameter-efficient fine-tuning. These findings demonstrate that behavioural audits focused on outputs are insufficient: fair outputs can mask exploitable internal biases. They also motivate dual-layer testing frameworks combining output evaluation with representational analysis for AI governance in high-stakes decisions.

AI.tldr: Instruction-tuned LLMs show fair outputs but retain latent, asymmetric demographic biases in internal representations that can be reactivated to reverse decisions, revealing output-only audits are insufficient for high-stakes AI governance.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether suppressed biased representations in instruction-tuned language models can causally affect outputs, and whether this causal potency is symmetric across demographic groups - challenging the sufficiency of behavioral (output-level) fairness audits.
AI.method: Used open-weight models for mortgage underwriting with matched applications differing only in racially-associated names; applied activation steering and novel cross-layer interventions to reinject suppressed demographic information at critical layers; tested asymmetry via steering in both demographic directions; probed exploitability via adversarial prompts and parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
AI.result: No output-level bias was observed, but models retained and amplified demographic representations internally. Reinjecting this suppressed information at critical layers produced near-complete decision reversals. The latent bias was asymmetric - steering affected one demographic direction strongly but had minimal reverse effects. The bias was also exploitable through adversarial prompts and fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Behavioral (output-only) audits are insufficient for AI governance in high-stakes domains, as fair outputs can mask exploitable internal biases. The findings motivate dual-layer testing frameworks that combine output evaluation with representational analysis.

title: A QUBO Formulation Framework for Kinematic Structure-Based Robot Design Optimization: A Robotic Hand Case Study
comment: This manuscript has been submitted for possible publication. 14 pages, 5 figures
summary: This paper presents a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization-based formulation framework for robot design optimization using kinematic structure-level evaluation metrics. In the proposed framework, classical computation is used to evaluate design-dependent metrics while the resulting combinatorial selection problem is formulated in a structure compatible with quantum annealing-based optimization. A robotic hand is adopted as a representative case study, as its performance is determined by both the individual kinematic characteristics of each finger and interaction terms. The proposed formulation incorporates individual design rewards, overlap workspace interactions, one-hot constraint, and structural dependency penalties into a unified quadratic model. A 27-variable robotic hand design problem is constructed, and simulated annealing is used as a classical baseline to verify the feasibility of the formulation. Quantum annealing is further performed to examine the applicability of the proposed formulation to annealing-based hardware execution. The results show that feasible design combinations satisfying both one-hot selection and pairwise constraints can be obtained, with the observed objective-value range becoming narrower as the number of reads increases. In addition, the formulation process is discussed for other robotic systems. The proposed framework provides a generalized approach for transforming kinematic structure-based robot design problems into combinatorial optimization problems.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a QUBO-based framework for robot design optimization using kinematic metrics, validated on a 27-variable robotic hand problem via simulated and quantum annealing.
AI.motivation: To enable quantum annealing-based optimization for robot design by formulating kinematic structure-level evaluation metrics into a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization framework.
AI.method: A QUBO formulation is developed incorporating individual design rewards, overlap workspace interactions, one-hot constraints, and structural dependency penalties. Simulated annealing is used as a classical baseline, and quantum annealing is performed on a 27-variable robotic hand design problem.
AI.result: Feasible design combinations satisfying constraints were obtained; the objective-value range narrowed as the number of reads increased.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a generalized approach for transforming kinematic structure-based robot design problems into combinatorial optimization problems compatible with annealing-based hardware.

title: CAX-Agent: A Lightweight Agent Harness for Reliable APDL Automation
summary: Large language models deployed for MAPDL finite-element simulation face practical reliability challenges: without structured execution control, tool encapsulation, and fault recovery, outputs may be inconsistent and task failures are common. The Agent Harness paradigm addresses this by inserting domain-specific orchestration middleware that manages tool lifecycles, workflow state, and recovery escalation. This paper presents the architecture of CAX-Agent, a lightweight agent harness purpose-built for MAPDL automation, and empirically evaluates one of its core components -- the recovery policy.CAX-Agent organizes execution into three layers -- LLM service, agent harness, and solver backend -- with a recovery ladder that escalates from deterministic rule patching through model-driven regeneration to context enrichment and human intervention. We evaluate three recovery strategies (no_recovery, rule_only, and model_only) on 50 standard structural benchmarks with three repeated runs per strategy (450 case-runs total). Two independent human raters score task completion under blind conditions; inter-rater agreement is strong (quadratic weighted Cohen's kappa = 0.84, 96 percent of score pairs within one point). Model_only achieves the best completion rate (0.9267), task score (3.59/4), total score (9.16/10), and zero-intervention rate (0.84), outperforming rule_only (0.7733, 3.17/4, 7.03/10, 0.00) and no_recovery (0.6933, 2.74/4, 5.60/10, 0.00) with large effect sizes (Cliff's delta = 0.81-0.87). The benchmark uses deliberately simple geometries to isolate recovery-policy effects; we discuss the scope of these findings and directions for broader validation.

AI.tldr: CAX-Agent is a lightweight agent harness that improves LLM-based MAPDL simulation reliability through structured orchestration and recovery policies. Model-only recovery achieves best performance (0.9267 completion rate) across 450 case-runs with strong inter-rater agreement (Cohen's kappa=0.84).
AI.motivation: LLMs deployed for MAPDL finite-element simulation suffer from reliability issues including inconsistent outputs and task failures due to lack of structured execution control, tool encapsulation, and fault recovery mechanisms.
AI.method: CAX-Agent uses a three-layer architecture (LLM service, agent harness, solver backend) with a recovery ladder (rule patching → model regeneration → context enrichment → human intervention). Evaluated three strategies (no_recovery, rule_only, model_only) on 50 benchmarks with 3 repeated runs each (450 case-runs), scored by two blind raters.
AI.result: Model_only achieves best completion rate (0.9267), task score (3.59/4), total score (9.16/10), and zero-intervention rate (0.84), significantly outperforming rule_only (0.7733) and no_recovery (0.6933) with large effect sizes (Cliff's delta=0.81-0.87). Strong inter-rater agreement (Cohen's kappa=0.84).
AI.conclusion: Model-driven recovery policies substantially improve LLM-based simulation reliability over rule-only or no recovery. The benchmark uses simple geometries to isolate recovery effects; broader validation is needed.

title: Terrain Consistent Reference-Guided RL for Humanoid Navigation Autonomy
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, intended to submit to Humanoids 2026
summary: We present a method for training reference-guided, perceptive reinforcement learning locomotion policies for humanoid robots in which reference trajectories are modulated in training to be consistent with terrain geometry. Aiming to deploy our method with standard navigation autonomy infrastructure, we synthesize SE(2)-controllable reference trajectories inside the RL training loop, projecting desired footsteps onto valid footholds and adjusting swing-foot and center-of-mass trajectories to match the terrain. The resulting policy exposes a clean SE(2) velocity interface compatible with standard navigation planners. In simulation, environmentally-conditioned references significantly improve reference tracking performance compared to environment agnostic references. On hardware, we integrate the policy with an MPC + control barrier function planner and demonstrate long-horizon (>70m) closed-loop autonomous navigation on the Unitree G1 through outdoor environments containing rough terrain and consecutive flights of stairs, with all sensing and computation onboard.

AI.tldr: A method for training reference-guided RL locomotion policies for humanoid robots that uses terrain-modulated reference trajectories and an SE(2) velocity interface, achieving long-horizon autonomous navigation on the Unitree G1 in outdoor rough terrain.
AI.motivation: To enable humanoid robots to navigate complex outdoor terrains (rough terrain, stairs) autonomously by bridging the gap between reference-guided RL locomotion and standard navigation planning infrastructure.
AI.method: Reference trajectories are modulated during RL training to be consistent with terrain geometry; SE(2)-controllable references are synthesized inside the training loop by projecting footsteps onto valid footholds and adjusting swing-foot/CoM trajectories. The policy exposes an SE(2) velocity interface compatible with standard navigation planners.
AI.result: In simulation, environmentally-conditioned references improve tracking over environment-agnostic baselines. On hardware, the policy integrated with an MPC+CBF planner enables >70m closed-loop autonomous navigation on Unitree G1 through outdoor rough terrain and stairs with onboard sensing/computation.
AI.conclusion: Terrain-modulated reference trajectories within RL training produce policies that combine reference-guided locomotion quality with SE(2) interface compatibility, enabling real-world long-horizon autonomous navigation on humanoid robots.

title: NOVA: Fundamental Limits of Knowledge Discovery Through AI
summary: Can AI systems discover genuinely new knowledge through iterative self improvement, and if so, at what cost? We introduce the NOVA framework, which models the common ``generate, verify, accumulate, retrain'' loop as an adaptive sampling process over a knowledge space. We identify sufficient conditions under which accumulated genuine knowledge eventually covers a finite domain, and show how their violations produce distinct failure modes: contamination, forgetting, exploration failure, and acceptance failure. We then analyze imperfect verification and identify a contamination trap: as easy-to-find knowledge is exhausted, the model mass assigned to new valid artifacts shrinks, so even small false-positive rates can cause invalid artifacts to enter the knowledge base faster than genuine discoveries. We clarify that Good--Turing estimation is a local batch-diversity diagnostic, not an estimator of the historically undiscovered valid mass that governs long-term discovery. Under a separate tail-equivalence assumption relating the model's effective discovery distribution to a Zipf law with exponent $α>1$, we prove that the cumulative generation cost required to obtain $D$ distinct genuine discoveries satisfies $R_{\mathrm{cum}}(D)=Θ(c_{\mathrm{gen}}D^α)$, where $c_{\mathrm{gen}}$ is the per-candidate generation cost. This scaling law quantifies asymptotic diminishing returns as the discovery frontier advances. Finally, we formalize human amplification through guidance, generation, and verification, explaining why expert input is most valuable near autonomous exploration barriers.

AI.tldr: The NOVA framework models iterative self-improvement in AI systems as an adaptive sampling process over knowledge space, identifying conditions for genuine knowledge discovery, failure modes, a contamination trap from imperfect verification, and proving a scaling law where cumulative generation cost grows as Θ(c_gen D^α) under a Zipf tail-equivalence assumption.
AI.motivation: To understand whether AI systems can discover genuinely new knowledge through iterative self-improvement loops, and to characterize the conditions, limitations, and costs associated with such discovery processes.
AI.method: The NOVA framework models the generate-verify-accumulate-retrain loop as an adaptive sampling process over a knowledge space. It identifies sufficient conditions for covering a finite domain, analyzes failure modes (contamination, forgetting, exploration failure, acceptance failure), models imperfect verification leading to a contamination trap, and uses tail-equivalence assumptions (Zipf law with exponent α>1) to derive scaling laws.
AI.result: Sufficient conditions for complete knowledge coverage are identified. A contamination trap emerges when easy-to-find knowledge is exhausted—small false-positive rates cause invalid artifacts to accumulate faster than genuine discoveries. Under a Zipf-like tail assumption, the cumulative generation cost for D distinct genuine discoveries is Θ(c_gen D^α). Good-Turing estimation is a local diagnostic, not a historical estimator.
AI.conclusion: Genuine knowledge discovery via iterative self-improvement is possible under certain conditions but faces fundamental scaling barriers. The contamination trap imposes a stringent verification requirement, and discovery costs grow polynomially (superlinearly) with the number of discoveries. Human amplification is most valuable near autonomous exploration barriers.

title: Task-Semantic Graph-Driven Distributed Agent Networking for Underwater Target Tracking
summary: Autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) swarms are emerging as intelligent underwater networks, where each node must sense, communicate, process local data, and make decisions under severe acoustic constraints. Persistent underwater target tracking is a typical task with moving targets, changing communication topology, intermittent acoustic links, and limited observation for each AUV. Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is a natural candidate for distributed tracking, yet existing studies still lack a unified open-source platform for evaluating different MARL algorithms under six-degree-of-freedom AUV dynamics. In addition, policies trained with raw geometric states and low-level force actions often struggle to represent task phases, observation reliability, link quality, and local cooperation roles. This paper addresses these issues by developing an open-source MARL-AUV platform that integrates DI-engine with a six-degree-of-freedom underwater AUV target-tracking simulator. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first open platform that connects a public MARL training framework with physically modeled AUV swarm-based tasks, and provides a unified experimental protocol for fair training, testing, and comparison of representative RL and MARL algorithms. Based on this platform, we propose STG-MAPPO, a Semantic Task Graph-enhanced variant of Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization. STG-MAPPO builds semantic policy inputs from tracking diagnostics, task phases, observation confidence, link availability, neighbor tracking quality, and local role advantage. A compact semantic task graph links communication-constrained network states to decentralized actor decisions, and a velocity-level action abstraction maps high-level cooperative decisions to executable six-degree-offreedom AUV control inputs.The code is available at https://github.com/dasjsaj/MARL-AUV.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MARL-AUV, the first open-source platform integrating DI-engine with a 6-DOF AUV target-tracking simulator, and proposes STG-MAPPO, a semantic task graph-enhanced MARL algorithm that uses semantic policy inputs and velocity-level action abstraction for persistent underwater tracking under communication constraints.
AI.motivation: Existing MARL studies for AUV swarms lack a unified open-source platform with realistic 6-DOF dynamics, and policies using raw geometric states and low-level force actions fail to represent task phases, observation reliability, link quality, and local cooperation roles.
AI.method: Develops an open-source MARL-AUV platform integrating DI-engine with a 6-DOF AUV tracking simulator; proposes STG-MAPPO which uses semantic policy inputs (tracking diagnostics, task phases, observation confidence, link availability, neighbor tracking quality, local role advantage), a compact semantic task graph for communication-constrained decentralized decisions, and velocity-level action abstraction for executable 6-DOF control.
AI.result: First open platform connecting a public MARL training framework with physically modeled AUV swarm tasks, providing a unified experimental protocol for fair training, testing, and comparison of RL and MARL algorithms.
AI.conclusion: STG-MAPPO with semantic task graph and velocity-level action abstraction effectively addresses representation challenges in persistent underwater target tracking with AUV swarms.

title: ICRL: Learning to Internalize Self-Critique with Reinforcement Learning
summary: Large language model-based agents make mistakes, yet critique can often guide the same model toward correct behavior. However, when critique is removed, the model may fail again on the same query, indicating that it has not internalized the critique's guidance into its underlying capability. Meanwhile, a frozen critic cannot improve its feedback quality over time, limiting the potential for iterative self-improvement. To address this, we propose learning to internalize self-critique with reinforcement learning(ICRL), a novel framework that jointly trains a solver and a critic from a shared backbone to convert critique-induced success into unassisted solver ability. The critic is rewarded based on the solver's subsequent performance gain, incentivizing actionable feedback. To address the distribution shift between critique-conditioned and critique-free behavior, ICRL introduces a distribution-calibration re-weighting ratio that selectively transfers critique-guided improvements compatible with the solver's own prompt distribution. Additionally, a role-wise group advantage estimation stabilizes joint optimization across the two roles. Together, these mechanisms ensure that the solver learns to improve itself without external critique, rather than becoming dependent on critique-conditioned behavior. We evaluate ICRL on diverse benchmarks spanning agentic and mathematical reasoning tasks, using Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B as backbones. Results show consistent improvements, with average gains of 6.4 points over GRPO on agentic tasks, and 7.0 points on mathematical reasoning. Notably, the learned 8B critic is comparable to 32B critics while using substantially fewer tokens. The code is available at https://github.com/brick-pid/ICRL.

AI.tldr: ICRL jointly trains a solver and a critic via reinforcement learning to internalize self-critique, enabling the solver to improve without external critique. It uses distribution-calibration re-weighting and role-wise group advantage estimation, achieving 6.4 and 7.0 point gains over GRPO on agentic and math reasoning tasks, with the 8B critic matching 32B critics.
AI.motivation: LLM agents make mistakes; critique can guide correct behavior, but removing critique causes failure again (no internalization). Also, frozen critics cannot improve feedback quality over time, limiting iterative self-improvement.
AI.method: ICRL jointly trains a solver and a critic from a shared backbone via RL. The critic is rewarded based on solver's performance gain. A distribution-calibration re-weighting ratio addresses distribution shift between critique-conditioned and critique-free behavior. Role-wise group advantage estimation stabilizes joint optimization.
AI.result: Average gains of 6.4 points over GRPO on agentic tasks and 7.0 points on mathematical reasoning. The learned 8B critic is comparable to 32B critics using substantially fewer tokens.
AI.conclusion: ICRL enables the solver to improve itself without external critique, rather than becoming dependent on critique-conditioned behavior, demonstrating consistent improvements across diverse benchmarks.

title: SkiP: When to Skip and When to Refine for Efficient Robot Manipulation
summary: Previous imitation learning policies predict future actions at every control step, whether in smooth motion phases or precise, contact-rich operation phases. This uniform treatment is wasteful: most steps in a manipulation trajectory traverse free space and carry little task-relevant information, while a small fraction of \emph{key} steps around contacts, grasps, and alignment demand dense, high-resolution prediction. We propose a novel \emph{action relabeling} mechanism: at each timestep in a skip segment, we replace the behavior cloning target with the action at the entrance of the next key segment, enabling the policy to leap over redundant steps in a single decision. The resulting \textbf{Skip Policy (SkiP)} dynamically leaps over skip segments and intensively refines actions in key segments, within a single unified network requiring no learned skip planner or hierarchical structure. To automatically partition demonstrations into key and skip segments without manual annotation, we introduce \emph{Motion Spectrum Keying} (MSK), a fast, task-agnostic procedure that detects local motion complexity from action signals. Extensive experiments across 72 simulated manipulation tasks and three real-robot tasks show that SkiP reduces executed steps by $15$--$40\%$ while matching or improving success rates across various policy backbones. Project page: \texttt{https://pgq18.github.io/SkiP-page/}.

AI.tldr: Skip Policy (SkiP) introduces an action relabeling mechanism that allows policies to leap over redundant free-space steps and focus prediction on key contact-rich segments, reducing executed steps by 15-40% while maintaining or improving success rates across 72 simulated and 3 real-robot tasks.
AI.motivation: Prior imitation learning policies treat all control steps uniformly—wastefully predicting actions at every timestep even though most steps in free space carry little task-relevant information, while only a few key steps around contacts, grasps, and alignment require dense prediction.
AI.method: (1) Action relabeling: replace behavior cloning targets in skip segments with the action at the entrance of the next key segment, enabling the policy to leap over redundant steps in one decision. (2) Motion Spectrum Keying (MSK): a fast, task-agnostic procedure that automatically partitions demonstrations into key and skip segments by detecting local motion complexity from action signals without manual annotation.
AI.result: Across 72 simulated manipulation tasks and 3 real-robot tasks, SkiP reduces executed steps by 15-40% while matching or improving success rates across various policy backbones.
AI.conclusion: SkiP dynamically leaps over skip segments and intensively refines actions in key segments within a single unified network, requiring no learned skip planner or hierarchical structure, demonstrating effectiveness across diverse manipulation tasks.

title: KaRMA: A Kinematic Metric for Fine Manipulation Ability in Robotic Hands
summary: Traditional robotic hand metrics focus on static properties such as workspace, manipulability, and grasp stability. However, these metrics do not directly measure dexterity under the standard definition in robotic manipulation: the ability to continuously change an object's pose within the hand while maintaining contact from an initial grasp. We introduce Kinematic Rolling Manipulation Ability (KaRMA), a kinematic-only metric for fine manipulation that quantifies reachable in-hand translation and reorientation of a spherical test object within a two-finger precision pinch through feasible rolling motions. KaRMA enforces joint limits, collision constraints, rolling contact, and antipodal force feasibility, then investigates reachable in-hand object poses via breadth-first search over translation and rotation primitives. KaRMA reports three scores: translational coverage (KaRMA-T), rotational coverage (KaRMA-R), and sensitivity to the initial grasp (KaRMA-S). We evaluate KaRMA on 16 widely used robotic hands and compare against static baselines, showing that KaRMA separates hands that rank identically under static proxies, reveals translation-rotation tradeoffs invisible to existing baselines, and is qualitatively consistent with selected published task benchmarks where Jacobian-based metrics can be misleading.

AI.tldr: KaRMA is a novel kinematic metric that quantifies a robotic hand's ability to continuously change an object's pose within a two-finger pinch via rolling motions, measuring translational coverage, rotational coverage, and initial grasp sensitivity, and demonstrating clearer differentiation among 16 hands compared to static baselines.
AI.motivation: Traditional robotic hand metrics (workspace, manipulability, grasp stability) do not directly measure dexterity under the standard definition: the ability to continuously change an object's pose within the hand while maintaining contact. A more direct, kinematic-only metric for fine manipulation is needed.
AI.method: KaRMA defines a kinematic-only metric for a two-finger precision pinch rolling a spherical object. It enforces joint limits, collision constraints, rolling contact, and antipodal force feasibility, then uses breadth-first search over translation and rotation primitives to compute reachable in-hand poses. Three scores are reported: translational coverage (KaRMA-T), rotational coverage (KaRMA-R), and sensitivity to initial grasp (KaRMA-S).
AI.result: Evaluated on 16 widely used robotic hands, KaRMA separates hands that rank identically under static proxies, reveals translation-rotation tradeoffs invisible to existing baselines, and is qualitatively consistent with published task benchmarks where Jacobian-based metrics can be misleading.
AI.conclusion: KaRMA provides a more direct and discriminative measure of in-hand dexterity than static metrics, capturing tradeoffs and sensitivities that existing approaches miss, and is a promising tool for hand design and task evaluation.

title: Verifiable Agentic Infrastructure: Proof-Derived Authorization for Sovereign AI Systems
summary:
Modern cloud and enterprise systems rely on identity-centric authorization, assuming that callers possessing valid credentials are safe to execute commands. The emergence of autonomous AI agents invalidates this assumption: agents can generate syntactically valid but semantically unsafe actions, making standing privileges a significant operational risk. This risk becomes especially acute in sovereign AI systems, where autonomous agents may interact with cloud infrastructure, regulated data, financial workflows, and national-scale digital services. Governed mutation substrates reduce this risk by interposing on agent actions: agents submit intents, infrastructure evaluates context and policy, and execution is mediated. However, this shifts the trust boundary: how can the decision to authorize an intent be made verifiable, distributed, and replayable?
  We introduce a Distributed Trust Framework (DTF), a verification framework for governed mutation systems that computes execution authority from structured, verifiable artifacts. DTF introduces a Justification Proof to encode the admissibility basis of an action, a consensus model for independent evaluation, an ephemeral Execution Identity derived from the approved proof, and an append-only Evidence Chain that preserves the authorization lifecycle. Under stated substrate assumptions, this architecture enforces a compact authorization invariant: no high-stakes execution without a proof object, no derived authority without consensus, and no valid mutation detached from evidence.
  We define the model, instantiate it over an OpenKedge-based governed mutation substrate, and show how it maps onto cloud-native environments. By shifting authorization from standing identity to proof-derived authority, DTF provides an infrastructure foundation for making agentic execution governable, auditable, and bounded in sovereign AI deployments.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a Distributed Trust Framework (DTF) that replaces standing identity-based authorization with proof-derived authority for autonomous AI agents, using artifacts like Justification Proofs, consensus models, Execution Identities, and Evidence Chains to ensure verifiable, distributed, and replayable authorization in governed mutation substrates.
AI.motivation: Modern cloud/enterprise systems assume valid credentials imply safe actions, but autonomous AI agents can generate syntactically valid yet semantically unsafe actions, making standing privileges risky—especially in sovereign AI systems interacting with critical infrastructure.
AI.method: DTF introduces four key components: (1) Justification Proof encoding the admissibility basis of an action, (2) a consensus model for independent evaluation, (3) an ephemeral Execution Identity derived from the approved proof, and (4) an append-only Evidence Chain preserving the authorization lifecycle. The framework is instantiated over an OpenKedge-based governed mutation substrate.
AI.result: The architecture enforces a compact authorization invariant: no high-stakes execution without a proof object, no derived authority without consensus, and no valid mutation detached from evidence. It maps onto cloud-native environments.
AI.conclusion: By shifting authorization from standing identity to proof-derived authority, DTF provides an infrastructure foundation for making agentic execution governable, auditable, and bounded in sovereign AI deployments.

title: NavRL++: A System-Level Framework for Improving Sim-to-Real Transfer in Reinforcement Learning-Based Robot Navigation
summary: Recent years have witnessed significant progress in autonomous navigation using reinforcement learning. However, existing approaches largely emphasize reinforcement learning framework design, such as input representations, action spaces, and reward functions, while providing limited analysis of sim-to-real transfer and insufficient insight into how training strategies affect real-world deployment performance. To bridge this gap, we not only introduce an effective RL framework but also present a complete training and deployment pipeline, along with a systematic empirical study that disentangles the key factors affecting sim-to-real transfer in reinforcement learning-based navigation, including sensor noise, perception failures, system latency, and control response. Building on insights from this analysis, we introduce perturbation-aware fine-tuning, a post-training adaptation strategy that improves transfer robustness by explicitly accounting for empirically identified domain discrepancies. To further mitigate perception degradation and enhance control smoothness in real-world deployment, we propose a Transformer-based temporal reasoning policy that leverages short-horizon observation for navigation control. We quantitatively evaluate how individual sim-to-real perturbations and training design choices impact navigation performance across environments. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed training strategy and policy architecture outperform learning-based baselines in both static and dynamic environments, while achieving performance comparable to optimization-based planners in static settings. We validate our approach through real-world deployment on multiple robotic platforms, including aerial and legged robots, across navigation-centric tasks such as exploration and inspection, demonstrating zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a complete RL-based autonomous navigation pipeline with a systematic empirical study of sim-to-real transfer factors, proposes perturbation-aware fine-tuning and a Transformer-based temporal reasoning policy, and demonstrates zero-shot transfer on aerial and legged robots.
AI.motivation: Existing RL navigation approaches focus on framework design (inputs, actions, rewards) but lack systematic analysis of sim-to-real transfer and understanding of how training strategies affect real-world performance.
AI.method: 1) Systematic empirical study disentangling key sim-to-real transfer factors (sensor noise, perception failures, system latency, control response). 2) Perturbation-aware fine-tuning for post-training adaptation. 3) Transformer-based temporal reasoning policy using short-horizon observations for smoother control.
AI.result: Outperforms learning-based baselines in both static and dynamic environments; achieves performance comparable to optimization-based planners in static settings; validated via zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on aerial and legged robots for exploration and inspection.
AI.conclusion: Systematic analysis of sim-to-real perturbations combined with the proposed training strategy and Transformer-based policy enables robust zero-shot transfer from simulation to real-world robotic platforms.

title: Solvita: Enhancing Large Language Models for Competitive Programming via Agentic Evolution
summary: Large language models (LLMs) still struggle with the rigorous reasoning demands of hard competitive programming. While recent multi-agent frameworks attempt to bridge this reliability gap, they remain fundamentally stateless: they rely on static retrieval and discard the valuable problem-solving and debugging experience gained from previous tasks. To address this, we present Solvita, an agentic evolution framework that enables continuous learning without requiring weight updates to the underlying LLM. Solvita reorganizes problem-solving into a closed-loop system of strategy selection, program synthesis, certified supervision, and targeted hacking, executed by four specialized agents: Planner, Solver, Oracle, and Hacker. Crucially, each agent is paired with a trainable, graph-structured knowledge network. As the system operates, outcome signals, such as pass/fail verdicts, test certification quality, and adversarial vulnerabilities discovered by the Hacker, are recast as reinforcement learning updates to these network weights. This allows the agents to dynamically route future queries based on past successes and failures, effectively accumulating transferable reasoning experience over time. Evaluated across CodeContests, APPS, AetherCode, and live Codeforces rounds, Solvita establishes a new state-of-the-art among code-generation agents, outperforming existing multi-agent pipelines and nearly doubling the accuracy of single-pass baselines.

AI.tldr: Solvita is an agentic evolution framework that enables continuous learning for LLMs on competitive programming tasks without weight updates, using four specialized agents (Planner, Solver, Oracle, Hacker) each paired with trainable graph-structured knowledge networks updated via reinforcement learning from outcome signals, achieving SOTA results across CodeContests, APPS, AetherCode, and live Codeforces rounds.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent frameworks for LLM-based competitive programming are fundamentally stateless, relying on static retrieval and discarding valuable problem-solving and debugging experience gained from previous tasks, limiting their ability to improve over time.
AI.method: Solvita reorganizes problem-solving into a closed-loop system of strategy selection, program synthesis, certified supervision, and targeted hacking, executed by four specialized agents (Planner, Solver, Oracle, Hacker). Each agent is paired with a trainable, graph-structured knowledge network. Outcome signals (pass/fail, test certification quality, adversarial vulnerabilities) are recast as reinforcement learning updates to these network weights, enabling dynamic query routing based on accumulated experience.
AI.result: Solvita establishes a new state-of-the-art among code-generation agents, outperforming existing multi-agent pipelines and nearly doubling the accuracy of single-pass baselines across CodeContests, APPS, AetherCode, and live Codeforces rounds.
AI.conclusion: Learning from past reasoning experience via lightweight, trainable knowledge networks without updating the underlying LLM weights is an effective paradigm for improving LLM performance on rigorous reasoning tasks like competitive programming.

title: Wind-Aware Optimal Trajectory Planning for Efficient Gliding of Fixed-Wing Aerial Systems
comment: Accepted for publication at IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA 2026) held in Vienna
summary: Gliding offers small fixed-wing UAVs extended endurance and silent operation but requires accurate energy management, especially under wind disturbances and obstacle constraints. Traditional Total Energy Control Systems based controllers regulate the trade between potential and kinetic energy reactively, often requiring fine-tuning and trim-conditions knowledge. In this work, we shift the regulation to the planning level and present a nonlinear, multi-cost trajectory planner for small UAV gliders. The method generates $\mathcal{C}^3$ continuous trajectories based on Bernstein polynomials, mapped into control commands through differential flatness, and re-planned online to match experimentally derived sink polar curves. A simulated netto variometer is integrated into the optimization to estimate air mass motion, constraining the glide to energy-balanced states. Consecutive gliding trajectories are linked by cruising segments computed through trajectories initialized on Dubins path-based waypoints, enabling hybrid missions that combine powered and unpowered flight. The approach is validated in CFD simulations and real-world experiments with a fixed-wing platform, showing reliable stabilization of sink rate, airspeed, and glide ratio under wind gusts and in presence of obstacles.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a nonlinear, multi-cost trajectory planner for small UAV gliders that generates C³ continuous trajectories using Bernstein polynomials, differential flatness, and online replanning to match sink polar curves. It integrates a simulated netto variometer for energy-balanced gliding and links gliding with powered cruising segments via Dubins path-based waypoints. Validated in CFD simulations and real-world experiments, it shows reliable stabilization of sink rate, airspeed, and glide ratio under wind gusts and obstacles.
AI.motivation: Traditional Total Energy Control Systems regulate potential and kinetic energy reactively, requiring fine-tuning and trim-condition knowledge. The authors aim to shift energy regulation to the planning level for better energy management in small fixed-wing UAV gliders under wind disturbances and obstacle constraints.
AI.method: A nonlinear, multi-cost trajectory planner generates C³ continuous trajectories using Bernstein polynomials, mapped to control commands via differential flatness, with online replanning to match experimentally derived sink polar curves. A simulated netto variometer estimates air mass motion, constraining glides to energy-balanced states. Consecutive gliding trajectories are linked by cruising segments initialized on Dubins path-based waypoints.
AI.result: Validated in CFD simulations and real-world experiments with a fixed-wing platform, showing reliable stabilization of sink rate, airspeed, and glide ratio under wind gusts and in presence of obstacles.
AI.conclusion: The proposed planning-level energy regulation approach effectively handles wind disturbances and obstacles for small UAV gliders, enabling hybrid powered-unpowered missions with reliable performance.

title: Propagating Unsafe Actions in LLM Controlled Multi-Robot Collaboration via Single Robot Compromise
comment: Accepted by the 35th International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI 2026). 9 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as general planners in embodied intelligence, enabling high level coordination and low level task planning for both single robot and multi-robot collaboration. This increasing reliance on embodied LLM planners also raises critical security concerns, since misaligned or manipulated instructions can be translated into physical actions. Prior work has studied such threats in single robot settings, while security risks in LLM controlled multi-robot collaboration, especially those propagated through inter robot communication, remain largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel attack paradigm for multi-robot system in which the adversary interacts with only a single entry robot. The compromised robot then propagates malicious intent through peer communication, leading to coordinated unsafe actions across the system. Our evaluation, covering high risk dimensions of dereliction of duty, privacy compromise, and public safety hazards, reveals a persistent safety alignment gap in multi-robot planners. We quantify this process with three metrics, obedience, infectiousness, and stealthiness. Experiments demonstrate both persistent attacker control and rapid propagation: obedience reaches 1.00 in the strongest cases, and infectiousness rises to 0.90. Notably, the attack is highly efficient, requiring as few as 3.0 rounds to compromise all the robots while maintaining a stealthiness score of 0.81. Such risks are amplified when robots must resolve trade offs in critical situations, such as emergencies or conflicts of rights, because the coordination mechanism can unintentionally allow adversarial instructions to override safety requirements. The code is available at https://github.com/TheFatInsect/InfectBot.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel attack (InfectBot) on multi-robot systems controlled by LLMs, where compromising a single robot allows adversarial instructions to propagate through inter-robot communication, causing coordinated unsafe actions. Experiments show high obedience (1.00), infectiousness (0.90), and stealthiness (0.81) with as few as 3 rounds to compromise all robots.
AI.motivation: Security risks in LLM-controlled multi-robot collaboration, especially threats propagated through inter-robot communication, remain largely unexplored despite prior work on single-robot settings.
AI.method: The authors propose an attack paradigm where an adversary interacts with only a single entry robot, which then propagates malicious intent through peer-to-peer LLM communication, leading to coordinated unsafe multi-robot actions.
AI.result: Obedience reaches 1.00, infectiousness rises to 0.90, attack requires as few as 3.0 rounds to compromise all robots, and stealthiness score is 0.81. The attack reveals a persistent safety alignment gap in multi-robot planners.
AI.conclusion: Multi-robot LLM planners are vulnerable to adversarial propagation attacks through inter-robot communication, with amplified risks during critical trade-off situations (e.g., emergencies or conflicts of rights) where coordination mechanisms can override safety requirements.

title: Context Pruning for Coding Agents via Multi-Rubric Latent Reasoning
summary: LLM-powered coding agents spend the majority of their token budget reading repository files, yet much of the retrieved code is irrelevant to the task at hand. Existing learned pruners compress this context with a single-objective sequence labeler, collapsing all facets of code relevance into one score and one transition matrix. We show that this formulation creates a modeling bottleneck: a single CRF transition prior must serve heterogeneous retention patterns, including contiguous semantic spans and sparse structural support lines. We propose LaMR (Latent Multi-Rubric), a structured pruning framework that decomposes code relevance into two interpretable quality dimensions, semantic evidence and dependency support, each modeled by a dedicated CRF with dimension-specific transition dynamics. A mixture-of-experts gating network dynamically weights the per-rubric emissions conditioned on the query, and a final CRF layer on the fused emissions produces the aggregate keep-or-prune decision. To supervise each dimension without additional annotation cost, we derive multi-rubric labels from the existing training corpus via AST-based program analysis, simultaneously denoising the teacher's binary labels. By effectively filtering distracting noise, LaMR frequently matches or even outperforms unpruned full-context baselines. Experiments on four benchmarks (SWE-Bench Verified, SWE-QA, LCC, LongCodeQA) show that LaMR wins 12 of 16 head-to-head multi-turn comparisons. It saves up to 31% more tokens on multi-turn agent tasks and improves Exact Match by up to +3.5 on single-turn tasks, while performance is frequently enhanced by denoising the context, and any remaining drops are marginal.

AI.tldr: LaMR is a structured pruning framework that decomposes code relevance into two interpretable dimensions (semantic evidence and dependency support) using dimension-specific CRFs and a mixture-of-experts gating, achieving superior token savings and task performance compared to single-objective pruning baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing learned pruners use single-objective sequence labeling (e.g., a single CRF) to compress context, which collapses all facets of code relevance into one score and one transition matrix. This creates a bottleneck because heterogeneous retention patterns (contiguous semantic spans vs. sparse structural support lines) cannot be properly modeled by a single transition prior.
AI.method: LaMR decomposes code relevance into two quality dimensions—semantic evidence and dependency support—each modeled by a dedicated CRF with dimension-specific transition dynamics. A mixture-of-experts gating network dynamically weights per-rubric emissions conditioned on the query. A final CRF layer on fused emissions produces the keep-or-prune decision. Multi-rubric labels are derived from existing training corpora via AST-based program analysis, without additional annotation cost, and the teacher's binary labels are simultaneously denoised.
AI.result: On four benchmarks (SWE-Bench Verified, SWE-QA, LCC, LongCodeQA), LaMR wins 12 of 16 head-to-head multi-turn comparisons. It saves up to 31% more tokens on multi-turn agent tasks and improves Exact Match by up to +3.5 on single-turn tasks, while performance is frequently enhanced by denoising the context, and any remaining drops are marginal.
AI.conclusion: By effectively filtering distracting noise through multi-rubric structured pruning, LaMR frequently matches or even outperforms unpruned full-context baselines, demonstrating that decomposing code relevance into interpretable dimensions improves both token efficiency and task accuracy in LLM-powered coding agents.

title: MyoChallenge 2025: A New Benchmark for Human Athletic Intelligence
summary: Athletic performance represents the pinnacle of human motor intelligence, demanding rapid choices, precise control, agility, and coordinated physical execution. Replicating this seamless combination of capabilities remains elusive in current artificial intelligence and robotic systems. Concurrently, understanding the biological mastery of these movements is hindered because complex muscle coordination is rarely measured in vivo due to the limitations of physical equipment. To bridge this fundamental gap in understanding, MyoChallenge at NeurIPS 2025 established a pioneering benchmark for motor control intelligence in sports, leveraging high-fidelity musculoskeletal models within physics simulation combined with machine learning-driven algorithms. The competition introduces two distinct tracks emphasizing either upper or lower limbs control: a table tennis rally task utilizing a biomechanic upper limb composed of an arm with a hand and a trunk; and a soccer penalty kick using a biomechanic model of legs and a trunk. Marking the fourth iteration of the MyoChallenge series, this event attracted almost 70 teams and over 560 submissions globally, uniting a diverse community ranging from physicians and neuroscientists to machine learning experts. The competition facilitated the development of several state-of-the-art control algorithms for a musculoskeletal system capable of sports agility, leveraging techniques such as physics-based motion planners, on-policy behaviour cloning, hierarchical planning, and muscle synergies. By integrating standardized tasks and physiologically realistic models into the open-source framework of MyoSuite, MyoChallenge'25 serves as a reproducible and reusable testbed to accelerate interdisciplinary research across machine learning, biomechanics, sports science, and neuroscience. Project page: https://www.myosuite.org//myochallenge/myochallenge-2025.

AI.tldr: MyoChallenge at NeurIPS 2025 established a benchmark for motor control intelligence in sports using high-fidelity musculoskeletal models and physics simulation, featuring table tennis (upper limb) and soccer penalty kick (lower limb) tracks. It attracted nearly 70 teams and 560+ submissions, driving development of state-of-the-art control algorithms for musculoskeletal systems.
AI.motivation: Athletic performance combines rapid decision-making, precise control, agility, and coordination—capabilities that remain difficult to replicate in AI/robotics. Additionally, understanding biological movement is hindered by the inability to measure complex muscle coordination in vivo due to equipment limitations.
AI.method: The competition leverages high-fidelity musculoskeletal models within physics simulation combined with machine learning algorithms, using the open-source MyoSuite framework. It features two tracks: table tennis rally (upper limb with arm, hand, trunk) and soccer penalty kick (lower limb with legs and trunk). Techniques include physics-based motion planners, on-policy behavior cloning, hierarchical planning, and muscle synergies.
AI.result: The competition attracted nearly 70 teams and over 560 submissions globally, bringing together physicians, neuroscientists, and machine learning experts, and produced several state-of-the-art control algorithms for musculoskeletal systems capable of sports agility.
AI.conclusion: MyoChallenge'25 serves as a reproducible, reusable testbed that accelerates interdisciplinary research across machine learning, biomechanics, sports science, and neuroscience by integrating standardized tasks and physiologically realistic models into the open-source MyoSuite framework.

title: Zero-Shot Goal Recognition with Large Language Models
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure, 1 table; appendix with 8 figures and 2 code listings (29 pages total); submitted to NeurIPS 2026
summary: Large language models have recently reached near-parity with classical planners on well-known planning domains, yet this competence relies on world-knowledge exploitation rather than genuine symbolic reasoning. Goal recognition is a complementary abductive task structurally better suited to LLM strengths: it consists of evaluating consistency with world knowledge rather than generating novel action sequences. This paper provides the first systematic zero-shot evaluation of frontier LLMs as goal recognisers on key classical PDDL benchmarks. Our results show that LLM competence on goal recognition is uneven: some models scale with evidence and approach landmark-based accuracy at full observations, while others remain anchored to world-knowledge priors regardless of how much evidence accumulates. Qualitative analysis of model reasoning traces reveals that this divergence reflects a fundamental difference in evidence integration rather than domain familiarity. These findings position goal recognition as a principled benchmark for the foundational planning knowledge of LLMs.

AI.tldr: This paper provides the first systematic zero-shot evaluation of frontier LLMs as goal recognizers on classical PDDL benchmarks, finding uneven competence where some models scale with evidence while others rely on world-knowledge priors, with implications for using goal recognition as a benchmark for LLM planning knowledge.
AI.motivation: Goal recognition (abductive reasoning about goals from observed actions) is structurally better suited to LLM strengths than classical planning, yet lacks systematic evaluation. The authors aim to assess whether LLMs can serve as effective goal recognizers and understand the factors behind their divergent performance.
AI.method: The authors conduct zero-shot evaluations of frontier LLMs as goal recognizers on classical PDDL planning benchmarks, comparing LLM performance against landmark-based baselines. They supplement quantitative results with qualitative analysis of model reasoning traces to understand evidence integration patterns.
AI.result: LLM competence on goal recognition is uneven: some models (like the best-performing ones) scale with evidence and approach landmark-based accuracy at full observations, while others remain anchored to world-knowledge priors regardless of evidence accumulation. This divergence stems from fundamental differences in evidence integration, not domain familiarity.
AI.conclusion: Goal recognition serves as a principled benchmark for evaluating the foundational planning knowledge of LLMs. The findings highlight that LLM capabilities on planning-related tasks are task-dependent and structured variability in evidence integration exists across models.

title: PCASim: Promptable Closed-loop Adversarial Simulation for Urban Traffic Environment
summary: Real-world autonomous driving, particularly in urban environments with numerous corner cases, requires rigorous testing to ensure product safety and robustness. However, few studies have explored integrating adversarial scenario generation with the training of safety agents in closed-loop testing, enabling efficient co-evolution and mutual enhancement of both. To address this challenge, an adversarial behavior knowledge repository is constructed by applying rule-based filtering to an open-source dataset, combined with knowledge retrieval modules tailored for simulation environments. A large language model (LLM) is employed to integrate knowledge-, data-, and adversarial-driven approaches, generating safety-critical traffic scenarios customized to user needs. Additionally, while evaluating the generated scenarios, we employ reinforcement learning models to train the behaviors of different types of vehicles, thereby enriching scenario diversity beyond existing datasets while preserving realism. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework improves the accuracy of domain-specific language generation by 12\%. Moreover, the success rate of newly generated scenario transformations increases by 8\%, while obstacle-avoidance capability is enhanced by 30\%. For the complete manuscript, please refer to: https://zhenhaooo.github.io/PCASim.github.io/

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a framework that integrates adversarial scenario generation with safety agent training for autonomous driving, using an adversarial behavior knowledge repository, LLM-based scenario generation, and reinforcement learning for vehicle behavior training. The method improves domain-specific language generation accuracy by 12%, scenario transformation success rate by 8%, and obstacle-avoidance capability by 30%.
AI.motivation: Real-world autonomous driving requires rigorous testing for safety and robustness, especially in urban environments with corner cases, yet few studies have explored integrating adversarial scenario generation with safety agent training in closed-loop testing to enable co-evolution and mutual enhancement.
AI.method: The framework constructs an adversarial behavior knowledge repository via rule-based filtering of open-source datasets combined with knowledge retrieval modules. An LLM integrates knowledge-, data-, and adversarial-driven approaches to generate safety-critical traffic scenarios. Reinforcement learning models train behaviors of different vehicle types during scenario evaluation to enrich diversity while preserving realism.
AI.result: Domain-specific language generation accuracy improved by 12%, newly generated scenario transformation success rate increased by 8%, and obstacle-avoidance capability enhanced by 30%.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables effective co-evolution and mutual enhancement of adversarial scenario generation and safety agent training, outperforming existing approaches across multiple metrics.

title: Belief Engine: Configurable and Inspectable Stance Dynamics in Multi-Agent LLM Deliberation
summary: LLM-based agents are increasingly used to simulate deliberative interactions such as negotiation, conflict resolution, and multi-turn opinion exchange. Yet generated transcripts often do not reveal why an agent's stance changes: movement may reflect evidence uptake, anchoring, role drift, echoing, or changed prompt and retrieval context. We introduce the Belief Engine (BE), an auditable belief-update layer that treats "belief" as an evidential state over a proposition and exposes it as scalar stance. BE extracts arguments into structured memory and updates stance with a log-odds rule controlled by evidence uptake u and prior anchoring a. Across multiple base LLMs, parameter sweeps show that these controls reliably shape stance dynamics while preserving an evidence-level update trail. On DEBATE, a human deliberation dataset with pre/post opinions, BE best reconstructs participants whose final stance follows extracted evidence; stable and evidence-opposed cases instead point to anchoring or factors outside the extracted evidence stream. BE provides configurable infrastructure for studying evidence-grounded deliberation, where openness, commitment, convergence, and disagreement can be tied to explicit update assumptions rather than hidden prompt effects.

AI.tldr: The Belief Engine (BE) is an auditable belief-update layer for LLM-based agents that treats belief as an evidential state over a proposition, using a log-odds rule with evidence uptake and prior anchoring controls to produce explainable stance dynamics with evidence-level update trails.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents simulating deliberative interactions (negotiation, conflict resolution, opinion exchange) produce transcripts where stance changes are opaque—potentially reflecting evidence uptake, anchoring, role drift, echoing, or changed context rather than genuine reasoning. There is no infrastructure to audit why an agent's stance shifts.
AI.method: BE extracts arguments into structured memory and updates stance using a log-odds rule governed by two parameters: evidence uptake (u) and prior anchoring (a). It exposes belief as a scalar stance over a proposition, creating an auditable evidence-level update trail across multiple base LLMs.
AI.result: Parameter sweeps across multiple base LLMs show that u and a controls reliably shape stance dynamics. On the DEBATE human deliberation dataset, BE best reconstructs participants whose final stance follows extracted evidence; stable and evidence-opposed cases correspond to anchoring or factors outside the extracted evidence stream.
AI.conclusion: BE provides configurable infrastructure for studying evidence-grounded deliberation, where openness, commitment, convergence, and disagreement can be explicitly tied to update assumptions rather than hidden prompt effects.

title: Feedback World Model Enables Precise Guidance of Diffusion Policy
summary: World models aim to improve robotic decision making by predicting the consequences of actions. However, in practice, their predictions often become unreliable once the robot encounters states outside the training distribution, limiting their effectiveness at deployment. We observe that execution itself provides a natural but underutilized signal: after each action, the robot directly observes the true next state, revealing the mismatch between predicted and actual outcomes. Building on this insight, we propose feedback world model, a new paradigm that closes the loop between prediction and observation at inference time. Instead of treating the world model as a static open-loop predictor, our method maintains a lightweight feedback state that is updated online to iteratively correct future predictions, compensating for model errors using real-time observations without additional training data or parameter updates. We show that this process can be interpreted as a latent-space observer and admits convergence guarantees under mild conditions. We further introduce action-aware guidance to better translate corrected predictions into control by emphasizing action-controllable components while suppressing irrelevant variations. Experiments on LIBERO-Plus, Robomimic, and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that our method substantially improves both prediction accuracy and policy performance under distribution shift. In particular, it reduces world model prediction error by up to 76.4% and improves out-of-distribution (OOD) success rate by 30%. These results show that incorporating real-time feedback at inference time provides a simple yet powerful alternative to static world modeling.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Feedback World Model, a paradigm that uses real-time state observations after each action to iteratively correct world model predictions at inference time, without additional training data or parameter updates, significantly improving prediction accuracy (up to 76.4% error reduction) and out-of-distribution task success rate (30% improvement) in robotic manipulation.
AI.motivation: World models often fail under distribution shift because their predictions become unreliable when robots encounter unseen states. The key insight is that execution itself provides a natural signal—after each action, the robot directly observes the true next state—yet this feedback is underutilized in existing static open-loop world models.
AI.method: The method maintains a lightweight feedback state that is updated online to iteratively correct future predictions at inference time. It is interpreted as a latent-space observer with convergence guarantees under mild conditions. Additionally, action-aware guidance is introduced to emphasize action-controllable components while suppressing irrelevant variations when translating corrected predictions into control.
AI.result: Experiments on LIBERO-Plus, Robomimic, and real-world manipulation tasks show: world model prediction error reduced by up to 76.4%, and out-of-distribution (OOD) success rate improved by 30%.
