We build a novel test suite designed to probe generalization to unseen documents via case and rule variations. Our findings indicate that legal reasoning is inherently compositional and that neuro-symbolic frameworks offer a more reliable and robust foundation for legal AI, as well as improved generalization to unobserved situations.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether LLMs' performance in legal reasoning stems from genuine ability or data contamination, and finds that neuro-symbolic systems outperform monolithic LLMs in robustness and generalization for tax law reasoning.
AI.motivation: To determine whether LLMs' strong performance on legal reasoning tasks reflects genuine reasoning ability or is artificially inflated by data contamination, and to identify more reliable approaches for legal AI.
AI.method: Conducted a comprehensive empirical study of tax law reasoning with a contamination detection protocol, systematically compared monolithic LLMs with hybrid neuro-symbolic systems (statutory text → formal representations → symbolic solvers), and built a novel test suite probing generalization via case and rule variations.
AI.result: Performance can be inflated by contamination; legal reasoning is inherently compositional; neuro-symbolic frameworks demonstrate superior reliability, robustness, and generalization to unobserved situations compared to monolithic LLMs.
AI.conclusion: Neuro-symbolic frameworks provide a more reliable and robust foundation for legal AI, with better generalization capabilities, than purely neural approaches.

title: Sign-Separated Finite-Time Error Analysis of Q-Learning
summary: This paper develops a sign-separated finite-time error analysis for constant step-size Q-learning. Starting from the switching-system representation, the error is decomposed into its componentwise negative and positive parts. The negative part is dominated by a lower comparison linear time-invariant (LTI) system associated with a fixed optimal policy, whereas the positive part is controlled by a linear switching system. The resulting bounds show that the negative-side LTI certificate is no slower than the positive-side switching certificate and may produce a faster exponential envelope. The analysis identifies a max-induced asymmetry in Q-learning error dynamics. This asymmetry is connected to overestimation: positive action-wise errors can be selected and propagated by the Bellman maximum, whereas negative errors admit an optimal-policy lower comparison. Finite-time bounds are provided for both deterministic and stochastic constant-step-size recursions.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a sign-separated finite-time error analysis for constant step-size Q-learning, decomposing error into negative and positive parts to reveal asymmetry where negative errors are dominated by an optimal policy LTI system while positive errors are controlled by a switching system, linking this to overestimation bias.
AI.motivation: To provide a more precise finite-time error analysis for Q-learning that accounts for the asymmetric dynamics of positive vs. negative errors, which is not captured by standard uniform bounds, and to formally connect this asymmetry to the well-known overestimation phenomenon in Q-learning.
AI.method: The paper uses a switching-system representation of Q-learning, decomposes the error componentwise into negative and positive parts, analyzes the negative part via a lower comparison LTI system corresponding to a fixed optimal policy, and analyzes the positive part via a linear switching system. Finite-time bounds are derived for both deterministic and stochastic constant-step-size recursions.
AI.result: The negative-side LTI certificate converges no slower than the positive-side switching certificate, potentially producing a faster exponential envelope. A max-induced asymmetry is identified where positive action-wise errors are selected and propagated by the Bellman maximum operator, while negative errors benefit from an optimal-policy lower comparison.
AI.conclusion: The sign-separated analysis reveals fundamental asymmetry in Q-learning error dynamics, providing tighter finite-time bounds than traditional approaches and formally linking the structure of Q-learning updates to overestimation bias.

title: ShopGym: An Integrated Framework for Realistic Simulation and Scalable Benchmarking of E-Commerce Web Agents
summary: Developing and evaluating e-commerce web agents requires environments that preserve meaningful task structure while enabling controllable, reproducible, and scalable scientific comparison. Existing methodologies force a tradeoff: live storefronts provide realism but are non-stationary, difficult to inspect, and irreproducible, while hand-built sandbox benchmarks provide control but cover only a narrow range of layouts, catalogs, policies, and interaction patterns. We argue that the core bottleneck is methodological: the field lacks a scalable way to construct evaluation settings that are simultaneously realistic, diverse, controllable, inspectable, and reproducible. We introduce ShopGym, an integrated framework for realistic simulation and scalable benchmarking of e-commerce web agents. ShopGym is a framework for constructing e-commerce simulation environments and grounded benchmark tasks. Its simulation layer, ShopArena, converts live seed storefronts into self-contained sandbox shops through anonymized shop specifications and a staged, validated generation process. On top of these simulated storefronts, ShopGuru synthesizes benchmark tasks across seven skill categories, grounding each task in the shop's catalog, navigation structure, policies, and interaction affordances. Together, ShopArena and ShopGuru produce self-contained, resettable, inspectable, and stable evaluation artifacts that preserve structural properties and agent-evaluation signals relevant to shopping tasks. We validate the framework through graph-based structural analysis and agent-based behavioral evaluation with 224 generated tasks across six sandbox shops: three constructed with synthetic data and three with real data. Our results show that the synthetic shops preserve key structural properties of live storefronts, with agent performance on synthetic shops positively correlated with performance on live storefronts.

AI.tldr: ShopGym is a framework for building realistic, controllable, reproducible e-commerce web agent evaluation environments by converting live storefronts into sandbox shops (ShopArena) and synthesizing grounded benchmark tasks (ShopGuru), validated through structural and behavioral analysis showing synthetic shops preserve live storefront properties.
AI.motivation: Existing e-commerce agent evaluation forces a tradeoff between realistic but non-reproducible live storefronts and controllable but narrow hand-built sandbox benchmarks; the field lacks a scalable methodology for constructing evaluation settings that are simultaneously realistic, diverse, controllable, inspectable, and reproducible.
AI.method: ShopGym consists of two components: (1) ShopArena, which converts live seed storefronts into self-contained sandbox shops via anonymized shop specifications and a staged validated generation process; and (2) ShopGuru, which synthesizes benchmark tasks across seven skill categories grounded in shop catalog, navigation, policies, and interaction affordances. Validation uses graph-based structural analysis and agent-based behavioral evaluation across 224 tasks on six sandbox shops (three synthetic, three real).
AI.result: Synthetic shops preserve key structural properties of live storefronts, and agent performance on synthetic shops is positively correlated with performance on live storefronts, validating the framework's ability to produce realistic yet controlled evaluation artifacts.
AI.conclusion: ShopGym enables scalable, reproducible, and controllable benchmarking of e-commerce web agents without sacrificing realism, addressing the core methodological bottleneck in the field.

title: Property-Guided LLM Program Synthesis for Planning
summary: LLMs have shown impressive success in program synthesis, discovering programs that surpass prior solutions. However, these approaches rely on simple numeric scores to signal program quality, such as the value of the solution or the number of passed tests. Because a score offers no guidance on why a program failed, the system must generate and evaluate many candidates hoping some succeed, increasing LLM inference and evaluation costs. We study a different approach: property-guided LLM program synthesis. Instead of scoring programs after evaluation, we check whether a candidate satisfies a formally defined property. When the property is violated, we stop the evaluation early and provide the LLM with a concrete counterexample showing exactly how the program failed. This feedback drastically reduces both the number of program generations and the evaluation cost, and can guide the LLM to generate stronger programs. We evaluate this approach on PDDL planning domains, asking the LLM to synthesize direct heuristic functions: every state reachable by strictly improving transitions has a strictly improving successor. A heuristic with this property leads hill-climbing algorithm directly to a goal state. A counterexample-guided repair loop generates one candidate program, checks the property over a training set, and returns the first case that violates the property. We evaluate our approach on ten planning domains with an out-of-distribution test set. The synthesized heuristics are effectively direct on virtually all test tasks, and compared to the best prior generation method our approach generates seven times fewer programs per domain on average, solves more tasks without using search, and requires several orders of magnitude less computation to evaluate candidates. Whenever a problem admits a verifiable property, property-guided LLM synthesis can reduce cost and improve program quality.

AI.tldr: Property-guided LLM program synthesis uses formal property checking and counterexample feedback instead of simple numeric scoring, reducing generation and evaluation costs while improving program quality. Applied to PDDL planning domains, it generates 7x fewer programs and requires orders of magnitude less computation than prior methods.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM program synthesis relies on numeric scores (e.g., solution value, test pass count) that offer no guidance on why a program failed, requiring many generations and evaluations. This increases LLM inference and evaluation costs.
AI.method: Instead of scoring programs after evaluation, the approach checks whether a candidate satisfies a formally defined property. When violated, evaluation stops early and provides the LLM with a concrete counterexample showing exactly how the program failed. A counterexample-guided repair loop generates one candidate, checks the property over a training set, and returns the first violation.
AI.result: On ten PDDL planning domains with out-of-distribution test sets, the synthesized heuristics are effectively direct on virtually all test tasks. Compared to the best prior generation method, the approach generates seven times fewer programs per domain, solves more tasks without search, and requires several orders of magnitude less computation for evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Whenever a problem admits a verifiable property, property-guided LLM synthesis can reduce cost and improve program quality.

title: Look Before You Leap: Autonomous Exploration for LLM Agents
summary: Large language model based agents often fail in unfamiliar environments due to premature exploitation: a tendency to act on prior knowledge before acquiring sufficient environment-specific information. We identify autonomous exploration as a critical yet underexplored capability for building adaptive agents. To formalize and quantify this capability, we introduce Exploration Checkpoint Coverage, a verifiable metric that measures how broadly an agent discovers key states, objects, and affordances. Our systematic evaluation reveals that agents trained with standard task-oriented reinforcement learning consistently exhibit narrow and repetitive behaviors that impede downstream performance. To address this limitation, we develop a training strategy that interleaves task-execution rollouts and exploration rollouts, with each type of rollout optimized by its corresponding verifiable reward. Building on this training strategy, we propose the Explore-then-Act paradigm, which decouples information-gathering from task execution: agents first utilize an interaction budget to acquire grounded environmental knowledge, then leverage it for task resolution. Our results demonstrate that learning to systematically explore is imperative for building generalizable and real-world-ready agents.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies premature exploitation as a key failure mode in LLM-based agents and proposes autonomous exploration as a critical capability. The authors introduce Exploration Checkpoint Coverage (ECC) as a verifiable metric, reveal that standard task-oriented RL produces narrow behaviors, and develop a training strategy interleaving task and exploration rollouts. The Explore-then-Act paradigm is proposed to decouple information-gathering from task execution, demonstrating that systematic exploration is essential for generalizable agents.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents often fail in unfamiliar environments due to premature exploitation—acting on prior knowledge without sufficient environment-specific information. Autonomous exploration is identified as a critical yet underexplored capability for building adaptive agents.
AI.method: The authors propose Exploration Checkpoint Coverage (ECC) as a verifiable metric. They develop a training strategy that interleaves task-execution rollouts and exploration rollouts, each optimized by corresponding verifiable rewards. Based on this, they propose the Explore-then-Act paradigm that decouples information-gathering from task execution.
AI.result: Standard task-oriented RL consistently produces narrow and repetitive behaviors that impede downstream performance. The proposed Explore-then-Act paradigm with interleaved training enables agents to first acquire grounded environmental knowledge via an interaction budget, then leverage it for task resolution.
AI.conclusion: Learning to systematically explore is imperative for building generalizable and real-world-ready agents, as it addresses the premature exploitation problem.

title: An Algebraic Exposition of the Theory of Dyadic Morality
summary: This paper provides an algebraic exposition of the theory of dyadic morality (TDM), a psychological model of moral judgment grounded in a simple two-node template: an intentional agent causing harm to a vulnerable patient. We formalize TDM using structural causal modeling (SCM) notation and identify three psychological operators (typecasting operator, completion operator, and valence-dependent inference mechanism) that extend standard SCM to capture how people compute moral judgments under constraints. We address scalability challenges arising from TDM's dyadic limitation, showing how moral cognition compresses multi-node scenarios through node collapse and sequential processing. Drawing on this algebraic framework, we demonstrate concrete applications to AI policy design: detecting conflicting obligations, structuring helpfulness policies to preserve user agency, and designing post-failure communication as causal interventions. Finally, we recommend scoped, contextual measurement of mind perception over universal averaging to operationalize the theory empirically. This algebraic formalization enables neurosymbolic AI systems to compute morality in a way that is both mathematically rigorous and faithful to human moral cognition.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes the theory of dyadic morality (TDM) using structural causal modeling (SCM), introducing three psychological operators (typecasting, completion, valence-dependent inference) to model moral judgment. It addresses scalability via node collapse and sequential processing, and demonstrates applications in AI policy design and empirical measurement.
AI.motivation: To provide a rigorous algebraic formalization of the theory of dyadic morality that enables computational implementation in neurosymbolic AI systems while remaining faithful to human moral cognition.
AI.method: The authors formalize TDM using structural causal modeling (SCM) notation, introduce three psychological operators (typecasting, completion, valence-dependent inference), and address scalability through node collapse and sequential processing.
AI.result: Demonstrates concrete applications to AI policy design: detecting conflicting obligations, structuring helpfulness policies to preserve user agency, and designing post-failure communication as causal interventions. Recommends scoped, contextual measurement of mind perception over universal averaging.
AI.conclusion: The algebraic formalization enables neurosymbolic AI systems to compute morality in a mathematically rigorous way that is faithful to human moral cognition.

title: Formal Methods Meet LLMs: Auditing, Monitoring, and Intervention for Compliance of Advanced AI Systems
summary: We examine one particular dimension of AI governance: how to monitor and audit AI-enabled products and services throughout the AI development lifecycle, from pre-deployment testing to post-deployment auditing. Combining principles from formal methods with SoTA machine learning, we propose techniques that enable AI-enabled product and service developers, as well as third party AI developers and evaluators, to perform offline auditing and online (runtime) monitoring of product-specific (temporally extended) behavioral constraints such as safety constraints, norms, rules and regulations with respect to black-box advanced AI systems, notably LLMs. We further provide practical techniques for predictive monitoring, such as sampling-based methods, and we introduce intervening monitors that act at runtime to preempt and potentially mitigate predicted violations. Experimental results show that by exploiting the formal syntax and semantics of Linear Temporal Logic (LTL), our proposed auditing and monitoring techniques are superior to LLM baseline methods in detecting violations of temporally extended behavioral constraints; with our approach, even small-model labelers match or exceed frontier LLM judges. Our predictive and intervening monitors significantly reduce the violation rates of LLM-based agents while largely preserving task performance. We further show through controlled experiments that LLMs' temporal reasoning shows a pronounced degradation in accuracy with increasing event distance, number of constraints, and number of propositions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes techniques combining formal methods (LTL) with machine learning to monitor and audit AI systems (especially LLMs) for temporally extended behavioral constraints throughout the development lifecycle, demonstrating superiority over LLM-only baselines in violation detection and reduction.
AI.motivation: To address the need for systematic monitoring and auditing of AI-enabled products and services across the entire AI development lifecycle, from pre-deployment testing to post-deployment runtime monitoring, particularly for detecting violations of temporally extended behavioral constraints like safety rules and regulations.
AI.method: Combines principles from formal methods (Linear Temporal Logic/LTL syntax and semantics) with SoTA machine learning to enable offline auditing and online (runtime) monitoring of black-box AI systems. Includes sampling-based predictive monitoring and intervening monitors that preemptively mitigate predicted violations at runtime.
AI.result: The proposed LTL-based auditing/monitoring techniques outperform LLM baseline methods in detecting violations of temporally extended behavioral constraints. Small-model labelers using this approach match or exceed frontier LLM judges. Predictive/intervening monitors significantly reduce violation rates of LLM-based agents while preserving task performance. LLMs show degraded temporal reasoning with increasing event distance, number of constraints, and propositions.
AI.conclusion: Formal methods (LTL) provide superior temporal reasoning capabilities for AI monitoring compared to pure LLM approaches, enabling effective offline auditing and runtime intervention for safer AI deployment.

title: Context, Reasoning, and Hierarchy: A Cost-Performance Study of Compound LLM Agent Design in an Adversarial POMDP
summary: Deploying compound LLM agents in adversarial, partially observable sequential environments requires navigating several design dimensions: (1) what the agent sees, (2) how it reasons, and (3) how tasks are decomposed across components. Yet practitioners lack guidance on which design choices improve performance versus merely increase inference costs. We present a controlled study of compound LLM agent design in CybORG CAGE-2, a cyber defense environment modeled as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP). Reward is non-positive, so all configurations operate in a failure-mitigation mode. Our evaluation spans five model families, six models, and twelve configurations (3,475 episodes) with token-level cost accounting. We vary context representation (raw observations vs. a deterministic state-tracking layer with compressed history), deliberation (self-questioning, self-critique, and self-improvement tools, with optional chain-of-thought prompting), and hierarchical decomposition (monolithic ReAct vs. delegation to specialized sub-agents). We find that: (1) Programmatic state abstraction delivers the largest returns per token spent (RPTS), improving mean return by up to 76% over raw observations. (2) Distributing deliberation tools across a hierarchy degrades performance relative to hierarchy alone for all five model families, reaching up to 3.4$\times$ worse mean return while using 1.8-2.7$\times$ more tokens. We call this destructive pattern a deliberation cascade. (3) Hierarchical decomposition without deliberation achieves the best absolute performance for most models, and context engineering is generally more cost-effective than deliberation. These findings suggest a design principle for structured adversarial POMDPs: invest in programmatic infrastructure and clean task decomposition rather than deeper per-agent reasoning, as these strategies can interfere when combined.

AI.tldr: In cyber defense POMDPs, programmatic state abstraction and hierarchical decomposition improve performance more cost-effectively than adding deliberation tools (self-questioning/critique/improvement), which can degrade performance when combined with hierarchy—a phenomenon called "deliberation cascade."
AI.motivation: Practitioners lack guidance on which design choices (context representation, reasoning, task decomposition) improve LLM agent performance vs. merely increasing inference costs in adversarial, partially observable sequential environments.
AI.method: Controlled study in CybORG CAGE-2 (cyber defense POMDP) with 5 model families, 6 models, 12 configurations (3,475 episodes), varying context representation (raw obs vs. deterministic state-tracking), deliberation tools (self-questioning/critique/improvement ± CoT), and hierarchy (monolithic ReAct vs. specialized sub-agents).
AI.result: (1) Programmatic state abstraction improves RPTS up to 76% over raw obs. (2) Combining deliberation with hierarchy degrades performance up to 3.4× worse return using 1.8–2.7× more tokens ("deliberation cascade"). (3) Hierarchy without deliberation achieves best absolute performance; context engineering is more cost-effective than deliberation.
AI.conclusion: For structured adversarial POMDPs, invest in programmatic infrastructure and clean task decomposition rather than deeper per-agent reasoning, as these strategies can interfere when combined.

title: Confirming Correct, Missing the Rest: LLM Tutoring Agents Struggle Where Feedback Matters Most
summary: Effective tutoring requires distinguishing optimal, valid but suboptimal, and incorrect student solutions, a distinction central to intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) but untested for LLM-based tutors. As LLMs are increasingly explored as conversational complements to ITS, evaluating their diagnostic precision is essential. We present a benchmark of seven LLM feedback agents in propositional logic using knowledge-graph-derived ground truth across 10,836 solution--feedback pairs and three feedback conditions. Models achieved near-ceiling performance on optimal steps but systematically over-rejected valid but suboptimal reasoning and over-validated incorrect solutions, precisely where adaptive tutoring matters most. These failures persisted across models regardless of solution context, suggesting architectural rather than informational limits. Moreover, accurate diagnosis did not reliably produce pedagogically actionable feedback, revealing a gap between diagnostic judgment and instructional effectiveness. Our findings suggest that LLMs are better suited for hybrid architectures where KG-grounded models handle diagnosis while LLMs support open-ended scaffolding and dialogue.

AI.tldr: LLM-based tutors excel at identifying optimal student solutions but systematically fail to distinguish valid-but-suboptimal from incorrect solutions, revealing diagnostic blind spots that suggest hybrid KG-LLM architectures over pure LLM tutors.
AI.motivation: Effective tutoring requires distinguishing optimal, valid-but-suboptimal, and incorrect solutions—a capability central to ITS but untested for LLM-based tutors. As LLMs are increasingly used as conversational complements to ITS, evaluating their diagnostic precision is essential.
AI.method: Benchmark of seven LLM feedback agents in propositional logic using knowledge-graph-derived ground truth across 10,836 solution–feedback pairs under three feedback conditions.
AI.result: Models achieved near-ceiling performance on optimal steps but systematically over-rejected valid-but-suboptimal reasoning and over-validated incorrect solutions. Failures persisted across models regardless of solution context, suggesting architectural rather than informational limits. Accurate diagnosis did not reliably produce pedagogically actionable feedback.
AI.conclusion: LLMs are better suited for hybrid architectures where KG-grounded models handle diagnosis while LLMs support open-ended scaffolding and dialogue.

title: Fully Open Meditron: An Auditable Pipeline for Clinical LLMs
comment: Preprint. 31 pages, 10 figures. Code, models, and data: https://github.com/EPFLiGHT/FullyOpenMeditron
summary: Clinical decision support systems (CDSS) require scrutable, auditable pipelines that enable rigorous, reproducible validation. Yet current LLM-based CDSS remain largely opaque. Most "open" models are open-weight only, releasing parameters while withholding the data provenance, curation procedures, and generation pipelines that determine model behavior. Fully Open (FO) models, which expose the complete training stack end-to-end, do not currently exist in medicine. We introduce Fully Open Meditron, the first fully open pipeline for building LLM-CDSS, comprising a clinician-audited training corpus, a reproducible data construction and training framework, and a use-aligned evaluation protocol. The corpus unifies eight public medical QA datasets into a normalized conversational format and expands coverage with three clinician-vetted synthetic extensions: exam-style QA, guideline-grounded QA derived from 46,469 clinical practice guidelines, and clinical vignettes. The pipeline enforces system-wide decontamination, gold-label resampling of teacher generations, and end-to-end validation by a four-physician panel. We evaluate using an LLM-as-a-judge protocol over expert-written clinical vignettes, calibrated against 204 human raters. We apply the recipe to five FO base models (Apertus-70B/8B-Instruct, OLMo-2-32B-SFT, EuroLLM-22B/9B-Instruct). All MeditronFO variants are preferred over their bases. Apertus-70B-MeditronFO improves +6.6 points over its base (47.2% to 53.8%) on aggregate medical benchmarks, establishing a new FO SoTA. Gemma-3-27B-MeditronFO is preferred over MedGemma in 58.6% of LLM-as-a-judge comparisons and outperforms it on HealthBench (58% vs 55.9%). These results show that fully open pipelines can achieve state-of-the-art domain-specific performance without sacrificing auditability or reproducibility.

AI.tldr: Fully Open Meditron is the first fully open pipeline for building LLM-based clinical decision support systems (CDSS), comprising a clinician-audited training corpus, reproducible data construction/training framework, and use-aligned evaluation protocol. Applied to five fully open base models, it achieves state-of-the-art domain-specific performance without sacrificing auditability or reproducibility.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based CDSS are opaque — most "open" models are open-weight only, withholding data provenance, curation procedures, and generation pipelines. Fully Open models exposing the complete training stack do not currently exist in medicine, hindering scrutable and auditable clinical decision support.
AI.method: They construct a clinician-audited corpus unifying 8 public medical QA datasets into normalized conversational format, plus 3 clinician-vetted synthetic extensions (exam-style QA, guideline-grounded QA from 46,469 CPGs, clinical vignettes). The pipeline enforces system-wide decontamination, gold-label resampling, and end-to-end validation by a 4-physician panel. Evaluation uses LLM-as-a-judge over expert-written vignettes calibrated against 204 human raters. Applied to 5 FO base models (Apertus-70B/8B-Instruct, OLMo-2-32B-SFT, EuroLLM-22B/9B-Instruct).
AI.result: All MeditronFO variants preferred over their bases. Apertus-70B-MeditronFO improves +6.6 points (47.2%→53.8%) on aggregate medical benchmarks, establishing new FO SoTA. Gemma-3-27B-MeditronFO preferred over MedGemma in 58.6% of comparisons and outperforms it on HealthBench (58% vs 55.9%).
AI.conclusion: Fully open pipelines can achieve state-of-the-art domain-specific performance without sacrificing auditability or reproducibility, demonstrating that transparency and high performance are compatible in medical LLM development.

title: FORGE: Self-Evolving Agent Memory With No Weight Updates via Population Broadcast
summary: Can LLM agents improve decision-making through self-generated memory without gradient updates? We propose FORGE (Failure-Optimized Reflective Graduation and Evolution), a staged, population-based protocol that evolves prompt-injected natural-language memory for hierarchical ReAct agents. FORGE wraps a Reflexion-style inner loop, where a dedicated reflection agent (using the same underlying LLM, no distillation from a stronger model) converts failed trajectories into reusable knowledge artifacts: textual heuristics (Rules), few-shot demonstrations (Examples), or both (Mixed), with an outer loop that propagates the best-performing instance's memory to the population between stages and freezes converged instances via a graduation criterion. We evaluate on CybORG CAGE-2, a stochastic network-defense POMDP at a 30-step horizon against the B-line attacker, where all four tested LLM families (Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, Grok-4-Fast, Llama-4-Maverick, Qwen3-235B) exhibit strongly negative, heavy-tailed zero-shot rewards. Compared against both a zero-shot baseline and a Reflexion baseline (isolated single-stream learning), FORGE improves average evaluation return by 1.7-7.7$\times$ over zero-shot and by 29-72% over Reflexion in all 12 model-representation conditions, reducing major-failure rates (below $-100$) to as low as $\sim$1%. We find that (1) population broadcast is critical mechanism, with a no-graduation ablation confirming that broadcast carries the performance gains while graduation primarily saves compute; (2) Examples achieves the strongest returns for three of four models, Rules offers the best cost-reliability profile with $\sim$40% fewer tokens; and (3) weaker baseline models benefit disproportionately, suggesting FORGE may mitigate capability gaps rather than amplify strong models. All evidence is confined to CAGE-2 B-line; cross-family findings are directional evidence.

AI.tldr: FORGE is a population-based protocol that evolves prompt-injected natural-language memory (Rules, Examples, or Mixed) for LLM agents via a Reflexion-style inner loop and a population-broadcast outer loop, improving average return by 1.7-7.7× over zero-shot and 29-72% over Reflexion on the CybORG CAGE-2 network-defense task across four LLM families.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether LLM agents can improve decision-making through self-generated memory without gradient updates, particularly in stochastic POMDP environments where zero-shot performance is strongly negative and heavy-tailed.
AI.method: FORGE wraps a Reflexion inner loop (failure trajectory → reflection → memory artifacts: Rules, Examples, or Mixed) with a population-based outer loop that broadcasts the best-performing instance's memory across the population between stages and freezes converged instances via a graduation criterion.
AI.result: FORGE improves average return by 1.7-7.7× over zero-shot and 29-72% over Reflexion across all 12 model-representation conditions; reduces major-failure rates (below -100) to ~1%; population broadcast is the critical mechanism while graduation primarily saves compute; weaker baseline models benefit disproportionately.
AI.conclusion: Self-generated population-based memory evolution (FORGE) effectively improves LLM agent decision-making without gradient updates; broadcast drives gains; Examples yields strongest returns, Rules offers best cost-reliability; evidence is confined to CAGE-2 B-line.

title: Prospective multi-pathogen disease forecasting using autonomous LLM-guided tree search
summary: Probabilistic forecasting of infectious diseases is crucial for public health but relies on labor-intensive manual model curation by expert modeling teams. This bespoke development bottlenecks scalability to granular geographic resolutions or emerging pathogens. Here, we present an autonomous system using Large Language Model (LLM)-guided tree search to iteratively generate, evaluate, and optimize executable forecasting software. In a fully prospective, real-time evaluation during the 2025-2026 US respiratory season, the system autonomously discovered methodologically diverse models for influenza, COVID-19, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Aggregating these machine-generated models yielded an ensemble that consistently matched or outperformed the gold-standard, human-curated Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) hub ensembles out-of-sample. The system successfully navigated data-scarce "cold start" scenarios for RSV. Moreover, controlled retrospective ablations revealed that optimizing log-scale distance metrics prevents reward hacking, while an automated judge-in-the-loop ensures structural fidelity to complex scientific theories. By autonomously translating epidemiological theory into accurate, transparent code, this framework overcomes the modeling labor bottleneck, enabling rapid deployment of expert-level disease forecasting at unprecedented scales.

AI.tldr: An LLM-guided tree search system autonomously generates, evaluates, and optimizes infectious disease forecasting software, matching or outperforming human-curated CDC ensemble models during the 2025-2026 US respiratory season for influenza, COVID-19, and RSV.
AI.motivation: Probabilistic forecasting of infectious diseases is crucial for public health but relies on labor-intensive manual model curation by expert modeling teams, creating a scalability bottleneck for granular geographic resolutions and emerging pathogens.
AI.method: The system uses LLM-guided tree search to iteratively generate, evaluate, and optimize executable forecasting software. It employs log-scale distance metrics to prevent reward hacking and an automated judge-in-the-loop to ensure structural fidelity to scientific theories.
AI.result: The system autonomously discovered methodologically diverse models for influenza, COVID-19, and RSV. Its ensemble consistently matched or outperformed gold-standard, human-curated CDC hub ensembles out-of-sample, and successfully handled data-scarce "cold start" scenarios for RSV.
AI.conclusion: By autonomously translating epidemiological theory into accurate, transparent code, this framework overcomes the modeling labor bottleneck, enabling rapid deployment of expert-level disease forecasting at unprecedented scales.

title: HoloMotion-1 Technical Report
summary:
In this report, we present HoloMotion-1, a humanoid motion foundation model for zero-shot whole-body motion tracking. A key innovation of HoloMotion-1 is to scale control-policy training with a large-scale hybrid motion corpus, where video-reconstructed motions from in-the-wild videos provide the dominant source of motion diversity, while curated motion-capture and in-house motion data provide higher-fidelity supervision and deployment-oriented coverage. This data regime enables HoloMotion-1 to move beyond conventional MoCap-only training and exposes the policy to substantially broader behaviors, capture conditions, and motion styles.
  Learning from such heterogeneous data introduces new challenges, including reconstruction noise, source-domain mismatch, uneven motion quality, and the need for temporal modeling under large behavioral variation. To address these challenges, HoloMotion-1 integrates large-capacity temporal modeling, a sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts Transformer with KV-cache inference for real-time control, and a sequence-level training strategy that improves learning efficiency on extended motion sequences. Extensive experiments on multiple unseen motion benchmarks show that HoloMotion-1 generalizes robustly across diverse motion types and capture conditions, significantly improves tracking accuracy over prior methods, and transfers directly to a real humanoid robot without task-specific fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: HoloMotion-1 is a humanoid motion foundation model for zero-shot whole-body motion tracking, trained on a large-scale hybrid motion corpus combining video-reconstructed motions, MoCap data, and in-house data, enabling robust generalization to diverse motions and direct deployment on real humanoid robots without fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: To move beyond conventional MoCap-only training and enable zero-shot whole-body motion tracking on humanoid robots by leveraging large-scale heterogeneous motion data from diverse sources (in-the-wild videos, MoCap, in-house data) to achieve broader behavioral coverage and motion diversity.
AI.method: HoloMotion-1 uses large-capacity temporal modeling with a sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts Transformer, KV-cache inference for real-time control, and a sequence-level training strategy to handle challenges from heterogeneous data (reconstruction noise, domain mismatch, uneven quality, large behavioral variation).
AI.result: On multiple unseen motion benchmarks, HoloMotion-1 robustly generalizes across diverse motion types and capture conditions, significantly improves tracking accuracy over prior methods, and transfers directly to a real humanoid robot without task-specific fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Scaling control-policy training with a hybrid motion corpus enables zero-shot whole-body motion tracking that generalizes beyond traditional MoCap constraints, and the proposed architecture addresses data heterogeneity challenges effectively for real-world humanoid deployment.

title: Residual Reinforcement Learning for Robot Teleoperation under Stochastic Delays
summary: Stochastic communication delays in teleoperation introduce signal discontinuities that undermine control stability and degrade control performance. Consequently, the conventional reinforcement learning (RL) methods struggle with the delayed observations due to the delay-induced observations, leading to high-frequency chattering. To address this, we propose a hybrid control framework, delay-resilient RL, integrating a state estimator utilizing Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) with a residual RL policy, which is resilient to stochastic delays. The LSTM reconstructs smooth, continuous state estimates from delayed observations, enabling the RL agent to learn a residual torque compensation policy that balances tracking accuracy with velocity smoothness. Experimental validation on Franka Panda robots demonstrates that our approach significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art baselines, ensuring robust and stable teleoperation even under high-variance stochastic delays.

AI.tldr: Proposes a delay-resilient RL framework integrating LSTM state estimator with residual RL policy to handle stochastic communication delays in teleoperation, achieving robust and stable performance on Franka Panda robots.
AI.motivation: Stochastic communication delays in teleoperation introduce signal discontinuities that undermine control stability and degrade performance; conventional RL methods struggle with delayed observations and cause high-frequency chattering.
AI.method: A hybrid control framework combining an LSTM-based state estimator (to reconstruct smooth, continuous state estimates from delayed observations) with a residual RL policy (to learn torque compensation balancing tracking accuracy and velocity smoothness).
AI.result: Experimental validation on Franka Panda robots shows the approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, ensuring robust and stable teleoperation under high-variance stochastic delays.
AI.conclusion: The proposed delay-resilient RL framework effectively mitigates stochastic delay effects in teleoperation, enabling stable control where conventional RL methods fail.

title: Hybrid LLM-based Intelligent Framework for Robot Task Scheduling
summary: This study introduces intelligent frameworks that use Large Language Models (LLMs) to improve task scheduling for construction robots. The LLM is fed with key data about the desired task, such as agent action abilities, and the desired end goal to be achieved. A well-balanced allocation strategy is developed, optimizing both time efficiency and resource utilization. Our system utilizes a Natural Language Processing interface to streamline communication with construction professionals and adapt in real-time to unexpected site conditions. We concurrently use two LLM agents, specifically generator (GPT-4) and supervisor (Gemma 3/Llama 4/Mistral 7b) LLM agents to provide a more precise task schedule. We evaluate the proposed methodology using a straightforward scenario and provide metric scores to prove the efficacy of the frameworks. Our results highlight that the implementation of LLMs is crucial in construction operational tasks including robots.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces LLM-based frameworks for construction robot task scheduling, using a generator-supervisor dual-agent system (GPT-4 with Gemma 3/Llama 4/Mistral 7b) that optimizes time and resource allocation via NLP interfaces, validated through scenario-based metrics.
AI.motivation: To improve task scheduling for construction robots by leveraging Large Language Models, addressing the need for intelligent, adaptive, and efficient allocation strategies that can handle dynamic site conditions and complex operational requirements.
AI.method: A dual LLM-agent framework with a generator (GPT-4) producing schedules and a supervisor (Gemma 3, Llama 4, or Mistral 7b) verifying/correcting them; uses NLP for human-robot communication, incorporates agent action abilities and end goals as inputs, and employs a balanced allocation strategy for time and resource optimization.
AI.result: Demonstrated efficacy through a straightforward scenario evaluation with metric scores, showing that the LLM-based framework produces precise task schedules and adapts in real-time to unexpected site conditions.
AI.conclusion: LLMs are crucial for enhancing construction operational tasks involving robots, providing both efficiency gains and adaptive scheduling capabilities through the proposed dual-agent architecture.

title: GAP: Geometric Anchor Pre-training for Data-Efficient Visuomotor Learning of Manipulation Tasks
summary: Learning visuomotor policies from scarce expert demonstrations remains a core challenge in robotic manipulation. A primary hurdle lies in distilling high-dimensional RGB representations into control-relevant geometry without overfitting. While using frozen pre-trained Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) improves data efficiency, it also shifts most task adaptation onto a small spatial pooling module, which can latch onto task-irrelevant shortcuts and lose geometric grounding when finetuned with few data samples. More broadly, pre-trained visual representations used for policy learning have been observed to struggle under even minor scene perturbations, highlighting the need for robustness-oriented inductive biases. We propose Geometric Anchor Pre-training (GAP), a simple, action-free warm-up stage that regularizes the spatial adapter before downstream imitation learning. GAP pre-trains the pooling layer on a lightweight simulated proxy task where object masks are available at no cost, encouraging the adapter to produce keypoints that lie on the object, cover its spatial extent, and remain sharp and repeatable over time. This yields stable geometric anchors that provide a reliable coordinate interface for few-shot policy learning, while keeping the VFM frozen. We evaluate GAP on RoboMimic and ManiSkill under severe data scarcity (15-50 demonstrations) and domain shift. A simple adapter regularized with GAP consistently outperforms stronger attention-based poolers and end-to-end fine-tuning, achieving 62% success on RoboMimic Can with 15 demonstrations (+16% over AFA), 63% on the long-horizon high-precision Tool Hang task with 50 demonstrations, and 61% on ManiSkill StackCube with 30 demonstrations (+11% over full fine-tuning). The proxy stage is lightweight and fully decoupled from downstream tasks, making it practical to reuse across environments and manipulation skills.

AI.tldr: GAP is a lightweight pre-training stage that regularizes spatial adapters in vision-based robotic policy learning by using a simulated proxy task with object masks, producing geometric anchors that improve few-shot imitation learning and robustness to domain shifts without modifying frozen vision foundation models.
AI.motivation: Learning visuomotor policies from scarce expert demonstrations is challenging due to high-dimensional RGB representations and overfitting. Frozen VFMs shift task adaptation to small spatial pooling modules that can latch onto task-irrelevant shortcuts and lose geometric grounding with few data samples, while also struggling under scene perturbations.
AI.method: Geometric Anchor Pre-training (GAP) is an action-free warm-up stage that pre-trains the spatial pooling layer on a simulated proxy task where object masks are available. It encourages the adapter to produce keypoints that lie on objects, cover spatial extent, and remain sharp and repeatable over time, providing stable geometric anchors for downstream imitation learning.
AI.result: Achieves 62% on RoboMimic Can (15 demos, +16% over AFA), 63% on Tool Hang (50 demos), and 61% on ManiSkill StackCube (30 demos, +11% over full fine-tuning). Outperforms attention-based poolers and end-to-end fine-tuning under severe data scarcity and domain shift.
AI.conclusion: GAP provides a simple, practical, and reusable pre-training strategy that improves geometric grounding and data efficiency for few-shot policy learning, with the proxy stage fully decoupled from downstream tasks.
